publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether the active components of working memory can operate without intention and outside conscious awareness
span.quote: It presents five studies that examine the relation between working memory and conscious awareness, with findings strongly suggestive of nonconscious, implicit WM.

span.label: can working memory operate implicitly, given that every existing WM task presupposes that it cannot
span.quote: We developed two new WM paradigms that allow for an examination of the role of conscious awareness in WM.

span.label: shows across five studies that patterns are extracted, maintained and used to bias responding without intention or awareness, and argues the field's view of working memory must widen to include an implicit mode
span.quote: Results from five studies show that WM can operate unintentionally and outside of conscious awareness, thus suggesting that the current view should be expanded to include implicit WM.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Results from five studies show that WM can operate unintentionally and outside of conscious awareness, thus suggesting that the current view should be expanded to include implicit WM.

span.label: implicit working memory
span.quote: This paper offers to extend our views of WM to include implicit working memory.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: We developed two new WM paradigms that allow for an examination of the role of conscious awareness in WM.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Incidental extraction of the pattern generates an anticipation of the next disk's location, which speeds responses when the anticipation is correct and slows them when it is violated
span.quote: Because of the hypothesized pattern-driven anticipations of the disks’ locations, RTs to last disks in Pattern sets (where pattern-based anticipations are veridical) should be faster than RTs to the last disks in Broken Pattern sets (where pattern-based anticipations are systematically misleading), with Control sets falling somewhere in between.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Conscious, intentional search for patterns produces frequent failures on the pattern-less majority of sets, and those failures interfere with the implicit extraction process
span.quote: Given the literature succinctly described above, the conscious search and its prominent failures are likely to interfere with the relevant implicit processes, and to diminish successful pattern extraction.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Discovering a pattern itself imposes a brief processing cost - an implicit 'aha' - that partly cancels the speedup it produces
span.quote: One possibility that comes to mind is that maybe there is an inherent slowdown upon the discovery of a pattern, as if the system takes a few milliseconds to develop an implicit “aha” experience.

span.label: the field's instruments are read as evidence about the field: every standard WM task is explicit, so the tasks record what researchers believe rather than test it
span.quote: We suggest to view these tasks as implicit, or indirect, measures of researchers’ beliefs regarding WM.

span.label: the question cannot be asked with the existing instruments because they presuppose its answer, so the paradigm has to be built before the experiment can exist
span.quote: Since existing WM tasks take as given that WM is predominantly conscious, they cannot be used to systematically address questions regarding the role of conscious awareness in WM.

span.label: a functional definition is adopted deliberately, so that whether the new task counts as a working memory task is settled by what it requires rather than by precedent
span.quote: To answer this question we adopt a functional perspective. Thus, a working memory paradigm is a paradigm that taps the functions of WM.

span.label: the design forecloses statistical learning by construction: pattern-following and pattern-breaking endings are equiprobable, so learning history predicts chance on the critical disk
span.quote: Note, furthermore, that in each block we keep the probability of a pattern-following last move equal to the probability of a pattern breaking last move (=.5). Thus, one’s learning history during the experiment should lead to chance performance on the fifth disk.

span.label: the first block is analysed separately as the empirical version of the same argument, since each pattern has appeared only once and there is nothing yet to have learned
span.quote: Although we argued above that the paradigm precludes statistical learning per-se, analysis of the data of the first block is an important empirical test of this assumption.

span.label: awareness is attacked from four directions rather than one — open debriefing, immediate reconstruction, forced-choice recognition, and a correlation between reconstructed and actual moves
span.quote: First, participants were asked explicit questions regarding the existence of patterns (self report). Second, they were asked to report whether they intended to extract patterns (self report). Third, participants were asked to immediately reconstruct the last set that they saw (free recall). Fourth, participants were asked to immediately recognize the last set that they saw (5-alternative forced choice).

span.label: in the fourth study awareness is manipulated instead of measured, which converts a null result about awareness into a predicted dissociation
span.quote: Instead of measuring awareness and intention, it manipulates them.

span.label: the excluded participants are turned into a test: if awareness drove the effect it should be larger in those who noticed the patterns, and it is smaller
span.quote: The basic idea of this analysis is that if the effect of patterns depends on awareness then it should be stronger for the participants in the Excluded condition, who were conscious of (at least some of) the patterns. Yet, the data does not support this suggestion.

span.label: a self-undermining fact — that every finite sequence follows some rule — is stated and then shown to bias the study against its own hypothesis
span.quote: In fact, every finite set of disks follows a mathematical rule (i.e., pattern). If participants extract this other pattern, rather than the one we intended them to, then the fifth disk in pattern sets actually breaks the pattern thus transforming this set to a broken pattern set (and vice versa for the broken pattern sets). What is important for our purposes here is that this factor leads to an underestimation of the effect of patterns.

span.label: the alternative account is not tested but reasoned through: imagine long-term memory doing this task, and it turns out to need the very operations attributed to working memory
span.quote: But these types of cognitive functions are usually attributed to WM (see Section 1.1), and parsimony suggests that we continue attributing them to WM, and not to LTM.

span.label: stimulus position is jittered specifically to block a strategy that would let attention narrow to the local level and bypass the global stimulus
span.quote: This measure was taken to prevent participants from strategically narrowing their attention, thus focusing on the components of the numbers (the local dimension), rather than on the numbers themselves (the global dimension).

span.label: the fifth study changes the material from spatial to algebraic so the claim rests on the function rather than on the modality
span.quote: Unlike in the first four studies the patterns here were not visual. Rather, they were constituted from the relations between the numbers (e.g., X n +1 = X n + 2). In this sense, then, the patterns are conceptual in nature.

span.label: Whether pattern naming, anticipation and control are done by working memory alone or by working memory interacting with long-term memory is left unresolved.
span.quote: Whether the processes of “naming” the patterns, creating anticipations for future locations, and controlling cognition, are done solely by WM or, like many other WM paradigms ( Baddeley, 2003 ; Gathercole, Pickering, Hall, & Peaker, 2001 ), involve the interaction of WM and long term memory, is an empirical question that we sadly leave for future research.

span.label: The comparison between excluded (aware) and included participants is heuristic rather than a formal test.
span.quote: We acknowledge that these analyses are heuristical in nature.

span.label: The unequal group sizes prevented a direct statistical comparison of aware and unaware participants.
span.quote: Given these huge differences in numbers we cannot directly compare the effects using an ANOVA.

span.label: The proposed implicit "aha" account of the asymmetry between speedup and slowdown is speculative.
span.quote: Admittedly, this idea is speculative.

span.label: the subject pool was contaminated by the laboratory's own research programme — participants arrived suspecting a hidden manipulation
span.quote: Thus, Hassin’s lab (where this study was conducted) runs many non-conscious goal priming studies. Towards the end of the academic year, many participants come to the lab suspecting that there is more to our experiments than meets the eye.

span.label: the excluded-participant analysis is conceded to be informal, compared by effect size because the group sizes forbid a test
span.quote: Given these huge differences in numbers we cannot directly compare the effects using an ANOVA. Hence, we use as heuristics the actual size of the effect in milliseconds and effect sizes.

span.label: the predicted pattern is asymmetric in a way the hypothesis did not anticipate: the slowdown is reliable and the speedup mostly is not
span.quote: The differences between Broken Pattern and Control sets were significant in three studies (1, 2, & 3), and marginally significant in one (4). The difference between Pattern and control sets, however, was significant in one study (4) and insignificant in the rest.

span.label: the explanation offered for that asymmetry is labelled speculation by the authors
span.quote: Admittedly, this idea is speculative. Regrettably, we leave the resolution of this issue to future research.

span.label: establishing that anything is non-conscious is acknowledged as never fully achievable
span.quote: Concluding that a process or a phenomenon is non-conscious is always a very difficult challenge.

span.label: whether long-term memory also contributes is left open, defended by parsimony rather than by data
span.quote: Whether the processes of “naming” the patterns, creating anticipations for future locations, and controlling cognition, are done solely by WM or, like many other WM paradigms ( Baddeley, 2003 ; Gathercole, Pickering, Hall, & Peaker, 2001 ), involve the interaction of WM and long term memory, is an empirical question that we sadly leave for future research.

span.label: block-level data exist for only two of the five studies because the analysis was thought of late
span.quote: The idea to examine the effects of Patterns in the first block came pretty late in the project. Hence, we have information about blocks only in Experiments 1 and 4.

span.label: whether implicit and explicit WM are one system in two modes or two systems is unresolved
span.quote: The putative differences between explicit and implicit WM, as well as other intriguing questions such as whether they belong to the same system or to two separate systems (cf. Keren & Schul, in press ), and what are their respective roles in higher order cognitive processes, are topics for future research.

span.label: the compound stimulus — a large digit built from small characters — borrowed so the cover task can be about the components while the pattern lives in the whole
span.quote: Each number was composed of either little X ’s or of little O ’s, and participants were asked to indicate as quickly as possible, using the keyboard, whether the number they saw was composed of X ’s or O ’s (cf. Navon, 1977 ).

span.label: the finding that conscious search damages extraction of complex structure, imported as the prediction that an explicit version of the task will show no effect
span.quote: One proposed explanation for these findings maintains that the conscious mind cannot apprehend complex structures of this sort, and so conscious search is bound to fail (cf. Reber, 1993 ).

span.label: a YOKED control condition in which the first three disk locations are random and only the fourth and fifth follow the pattern - the mirror image of the experimental condition, matched on everything except where the regularity sits
span.quote: in the yoked Control condition the locations of the first three disks are randomly determined, but the fourth and fifth follow the pattern.

span.label: working memory — defined functionally, by the operations a task demands, rather than by membership in the established task set; the move that makes the new paradigm admissible
span.quote: To answer this question we adopt a functional perspective. Thus, a working memory paradigm is a paradigm that taps the functions of WM.

span.label: working memory — as the field's tasks define it in practice: materials explicitly presented and explicitly manipulated
span.quote: In all of them participants are explicitly presented with materials that they are explicitly asked to manipulate (e.g., they are instructed to memorize, rehearse, compare, subtract, and so on).

span.label: implicit — as unintentional (not deliberately recruited) versus as unconscious (not available to awareness); the paper claims both and tests them separately
span.quote: we suggest that the processes that were identified above as underlying (or constituting) WM can be recruited without conscious intention, and that they can then go on to operate non-consciously

span.label: conscious involvement in WM — as attaching to some components (Cowan, Baddeley) versus to all active operations (Baars and Franklin)
span.quote: Baars (1997) went one step further by postulating that conscious awareness is involved in all WM input, output, and voluntary operations, as in explicit problem solving.

span.label: pattern — visual, drawn by connecting disk locations, versus conceptual, constituted by the algebraic relation between successive numbers
span.quote: Unlike in the first four studies the patterns here were not visual. Rather, they were constituted from the relations between the numbers (e.g., X n +1 = X n + 2). In this sense, then, the patterns are conceptual in nature.

span.label: pattern — the one the experimenters built in, versus the mathematical rule any finite sequence trivially satisfies; the second sense makes every broken pattern a pattern
span.quote: The fact that the fifth disk in Broken Pattern sets did not follow our intended pattern does not mean that it did not follow some other pattern.

span.label: implicit working memory — as a mode of one system versus as a separate system; the paper says which it assumes and why, and leaves the question open
span.quote: If this is the case, then parsimony suggests that we view implicit working memory as a mode of operation of WM, at least until new data suggest otherwise.

span.label: extraction — deliberately left open to cover identification and recognition, because the argument needs only the operations, not the label
span.quote: By “extraction” we do not mean to rule out other theoretical alternatives such as “identification” or “recognition”.

span.label: replicates → McKone (1995) verbal and Maljkovic & Nakayama (1994) visual implicit short-term memory findings
span.quote: McKone’s paradigm is verbal in nature whereas Maljkovic’s paradigm is visual in nature; the results of the current studies replicate both findings in new paradigms.

span.label: extends → previous implicit short-term memory findings (McKone; Maljkovic and colleagues)
span.quote: The current results offer a significant extension to the pervious findings by suggesting that other processes that are considered central to WM can occur implicitly (see p. 4).

span.label: critiques → the prevalent view that the active components of working memory are intentional and conscious, and the task set that encodes it
span.quote: The prevalent view holds that active components of WM are predominantly intentional and conscious. This conception is oftentimes expressed explicitly, but it is best reflected in the nature of major WM tasks: All of them are blatantly explicit.

span.label: contradicts → Baars and Franklin's claim that all active components of classical working memory are conscious
span.quote: Similarly, in a more recent paper Baars and Franklin argued that “all active components of classical working memory are conscious: input, rehearsal, visuospatial operations, recall and report.” ( Baars & Franklin, 2003 , p. 170).

span.label: extends → McKone's and Maljkovic's demonstrations of implicit short-term memory, from maintenance alone to updating, computation and control
span.quote: The current results offer a significant extension to the pervious findings by suggesting that other processes that are considered central to WM can occur implicitly (see p. 4).

span.label: supports → the social-cognition literature showing that high-order processes and goal pursuit can occur non-consciously
span.quote: Yet, recent research in social cognition has established that high-order cognitive processes in general, and goal pursuit in particular, can occur non-consciously (for recent overviews of this literature see Bargh (2006) and Hassin, Uleman, and Bargh (2005) ).

span.label: extends → models of non-conscious high-order processes, which currently contain no working memory component
span.quote: Existing models of high order non-conscious processes do not involve WM, a fact that should not come as a surprise given the traditional equation of WM with conscious awareness.

span.label: builds-on → the implicit-learning finding that directing attention to a complex structure can prevent its extraction
span.quote: Previous findings in the long-term implicit learning literature suggest that drawing people’s attention to the existence of complex structures in their environment may interfere with the extraction of these patterns (e.g., Berry & Broadbent, 1988 ; Brooks, 1978 ; Reber, 1976 ).

span.label: implicit working memory —part-of→ Working Memory
span.quote: Results from five studies show that WM can operate unintentionally and outside of conscious awareness, thus suggesting that the current view should be expanded to include implicit WM.

span.label: implicit working memory —distinct-from→ implicit learning
span.quote: We conclude, then, that evidence for pattern extraction in this paradigm cannot be merely attributed to implicit learning.

span.label: implicit working memory —distinct-from→ long term memory
span.quote: But these types of cognitive functions are usually attributed to WM (see Section 1.1), and parsimony suggests that we continue attributing them to WM, and not to LTM.

span.label: Pattern sets —contrasted-with→ Broken Pattern
span.quote: In the yoked Broken Pattern condition the locations of the first four disks in a set follow the same pattern (e.g., zigzag), but the location of the fifth disk does not

span.label: pattern extraction —operationalised-as→ reaction time
span.quote: The dependent measure of interest is thus reaction time to the last disks in Pattern, Broken Pattern and Control sets.

span.label: pattern extraction —causes→ anticipations
span.quote: If participants extract the pattern during the first four disks of a Pattern set, they can correctly anticipate the location of the last disk in that particular set.

span.label: conscious awareness —operationalised-as→ immediate reconstruction
span.quote: We argue that the correlation between the lists is an indication of participants’ awareness: If participants were aware of the sets then they should have been be able to fully reconstruct it, yielding a perfect correlation; no awareness might yield chance-based reconstructions, and hence no correlation.

span.label: conscious awareness —operationalised-as→ recognition test
span.quote: Immediately following their last response to this set participants were given a recognition test.

span.label: Implicit condition —contrasted-with→ Explicit condition
span.quote: Thus, participants in one group (the Implicit condition) received the same instructions as those of studies 1–3, while participants in the other group (the Explicit condition) were explicitly told about the existence of visual patterns and were encouraged to find them.

span.label: repetition priming —contrasted-with→ popout
span.quote: Whether these lines of investigation look at two different implicit mechanisms – reminiscent of the phonological loop and the visuospatial sketchpad ( Baddeley & Hitch, 1974 ) – or at a more general short term implicit memory system(s) is still an open question.

span.label: executive functions —part-of→ Working Memory
span.quote: The latter processes include attending and inhibiting, scheduling, monitoring and planning (cf. Smith & Jonides, 1999 ).

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: A 3 (Pattern: Pattern, Broken Pattern, Control) × 2 (Block) within subjects’ ANOVA revealed that, as hypothesized, RTs in the Pattern condition ( M = 528 ms, SD = 48) were considerably shorter than those for the Broken pattern condition ( M = 565 ms, SD = 62) with RTs for control sets falling in between ( M = 532 ms, SD = 48), F (2, 30) = 5.55, p < .01, MSE = 2.41, partial η 2 = .27.

span.label: repeated-measures ANOVA
span.quote: Participants’ mean RTs to the three conditions were subjected to a repeated measures ANOVA.

span.label: t-test (planned comparisons)
span.quote: Planned comparisons revealed that the difference between the Pattern and Broken Pattern conditions was significant, t (15) = 3.07, p < .01, as was the difference between the Control and Broken Pattern conditions, t (15) = 2.85, p < .02.

span.label: effect size
span.quote: Secondly, the effect size in the Included condition was 50% bigger than that in the Excluded condition (partial η 2 = .20 and .14, respectively).

span.label: correlation
span.quote: The individual correlations ranged from –.54 to +.49, and none of them significantly differed from zero, ps > .2.

span.label: standard deviation (outlier trimming)
span.quote: Incorrect responses, as well as responses that were faster than 200 ms or slower than three SDs from the mean, were discarded from analyses (4.3%).

span.label: interaction test in a mixed factorial design
span.term: interaction test in a mixed factorial design
span.quote: Crucially for the current concerns, a significant interaction between Instructions and Pattern emerged, F (2, 82) = 5.32, p < .01, MSE = 1.79, partial η 2 = .12.

span.quote: A 3 (Pattern: Pattern, Broken Pattern, Control) × 2 (Block) within subjects’ ANOVA revealed that, as hypothesized, RTs in the Pattern condition

span.quote: Planned comparisons revealed that the difference between the Pattern and Broken Pattern conditions was significant, t (15) = 3.07, p < .01

span.label: MSE
mixed design
span.quote: The current study employs a 2 (Instructions: Implicit vs. Explicit; between participants) × 3 (Pattern: Pattern, Control, Broken Pattern; within participants), × 2 (Block) mixed design.

span.label: one tailed
span.quote: whereas the difference between pattern and control sets only approaches significance ( p < .09, one tailed)

span.label: correlation
span.quote: The individual correlations ranged from –.54 to +.49, and none of them significantly differed from zero, ps > .2.

span.label: Participants responded faster to the final disk of pattern-following sets than to pattern-breaking sets, with control sets in between, even though the patterns were irrelevant to their explicit task.
span.quote: A 3 (Pattern: Pattern, Broken Pattern, Control) × 2 (Block) within subjects’ ANOVA revealed that, as hypothesized, RTs in the Pattern condition ( M = 528 ms, SD = 48) were considerably shorter than those for the Broken pattern condition ( M = 565 ms, SD = 62) with RTs for control sets falling in between ( M = 532 ms, SD = 48), F (2, 30) = 5.55, p < .01, MSE = 2.41, partial η 2 = .27.

span.label: The pattern effect was already present in the very first block, which rules out gradual implicit learning as its source.
span.quote: Importantly, pattern extraction occurred on the first block, thus ruling out implicit learning as an alternative explanation of the results.

span.label: Judges could detect no awareness of the patterns in participants' immediate reconstructions of the last set they had seen.
span.quote: Both judges concluded that none of the participants had been aware of the patterns.

span.label: Recognition of the last pattern set was exactly at chance, corroborating that participants were unaware of the patterns.
span.quote: Out of the remaining 30 participants only 5, or 20%, correctly recognized the set.

span.label: The pattern effect appeared only when instructions kept the task incidental; telling participants to search for patterns abolished it.
span.quote: As hypothesized, the interaction consisted of a significant effect of Pattern in the Implicit condition, F (2, 32) = 10.75, p < .001, MSE = 1.12, partial η 2 = .40, and no effect of Pattern in the Explicit condition F = 1.1 (for means see Table 2 ).

span.label: The effect replicated conceptually with numeric (algebraic) rather than visuospatial patterns.
span.quote: As hypothesized, RTs for the fourth terms in the Pattern condition were significantly shorter than those in the Broken Pattern condition ( M = 547 ms, SD = 84 vs. M = 561 ms, SD = 82) t (25) = 2.35, p < .05.

span.label: The effect is asymmetric: the slowdown on broken-pattern sets is more reliable than the speedup on pattern sets.
span.quote: Coupled with the analyses described above this suggests to us that there are both speedup and slowdown, but the latter is stronger than the former.

span.label: Participants excluded for reporting awareness showed a smaller, not larger, pattern effect than the unaware participants.
span.quote: First, whereas the difference between broken pattern and pattern RTs was 31 ms in the Included condition, it was only 17 ms in the Excluded

span.label: An accompanying fMRI analysis found right prefrontal activation for pattern relative to control sets.
span.quote: As hypothesized, fMRI analyses revealed increased activation in the right PFC during the Pattern sets relative to the Control sets.

span.label: responses to the last disk were faster after an intact pattern than after a broken one, with controls in between
span.quote: RTs in the Pattern condition ( M = 528 ms, SD = 48) were considerably shorter than those for the Broken pattern condition ( M = 565 ms, SD = 62) with RTs for control sets falling in between ( M = 532 ms, SD = 48), F (2, 30) = 5.55, p < .01, MSE = 2.41, partial η 2 = .27

span.label: the effect was already present in the first block, where each pattern had appeared only once, ruling out statistical learning
span.quote: And indeed, a repeated measures ANOVA on this block revealed a highly significant effect of Pattern, F (2, 30) = 7.17, p < .01, MSE = 1.55, partial η 2 = .32.

span.label: two judges found no participant aware of the patterns, and reconstruction correlations with the actual moves did not differ from zero
span.quote: The individual correlations ranged from –.54 to +.49, and none of them significantly differed from zero, ps > .2. The mean correlation did not significantly deviate from zero too, M = – .08, SD = .33, p = .42.

span.label: recognition of the last set was exactly at chance — 5 of 30, or 20%, in a five-alternative test
span.quote: Out of the remaining 30 participants only 5, or 20%, correctly recognized the set. This proportion is exactly that expected by chance.

span.label: the effect held even when only participants who failed the recognition test were analysed
span.quote: Although recognition rate is at chance level, we also conducted similar analyses only for those participants who could not recognize (or correctly guess) the last set that they have seen. These analyses yielded a similar pattern of results.

span.label: telling participants the patterns exist abolished the effect — a significant Instructions by Pattern interaction, with the effect present implicitly and absent explicitly
span.quote: As hypothesized, the interaction consisted of a significant effect of Pattern in the Implicit condition, F (2, 32) = 10.75, p < .001, MSE = 1.12, partial η 2 = .40, and no effect of Pattern in the Explicit condition F = 1.1 (for means see Table 2 ).

span.label: the effect replicated with algebraic rather than spatial patterns, in sets of one-digit numbers
span.quote: As hypothesized, RTs for the fourth terms in the Pattern condition were significantly shorter than those in the Broken Pattern condition ( M = 547 ms, SD = 84 vs. M = 561 ms, SD = 82) t (25) = 2.35, p < .05.

span.label: the participants excluded for being aware showed a SMALLER effect than those included — 17 ms against 31 ms, with effect size half again as large in the unaware group
span.quote: First, whereas the difference between broken pattern and pattern RTs was 31 ms in the Included condition, it was only 17 ms in the Excluded (similar differences between the Excluded and Included conditions are obtained when one compares the broken patterns and the control ones). Secondly, the effect size in the Included condition was 50% bigger than that in the Excluded condition (partial η 2 = .20 and .14, respectively).

span.label: the effect is asymmetric: the slowdown after a broken pattern is reliable, the speedup after an intact one mostly is not
span.quote: Coupled with the analyses described above this suggests to us that there are both speedup and slowdown, but the latter is stronger than the former.

span.label: the companion fMRI work found right prefrontal activation — inferior frontal sulcus, cingulate sulcus and frontal eye field — during pattern sets relative to controls
span.quote: As hypothesized, fMRI analyses revealed increased activation in the right PFC during the Pattern sets relative to the Control sets.

span.label: prior work found implicit short-term components in repetition priming lasting about 8 s, and in visual popout lasting 15–30 s
span.quote: This effect lasts for 15–30 s, suggesting that the short term visual memory of the popout feature improves performance.

span.label: in study 2 the pattern effect replicated with faster overall responding, 462 ms against 489 ms for broken patterns
span.quote: Replicating the results of the first study, participants were faster to react to pattern sets than to broken pattern sets, with control sets falling in between ( M = 462 ms, SD = 61, M = 489 ms, SD = 66, and M = 465 ms, SD = 78, respectively), F (2, 30) = 4.62, p < .05, MSE = .72, partial η 2 = .24.

span.label: working memory paradigm (functional definition)
span.quote: Thus, a working memory paradigm is a paradigm that taps the functions of WM.

span.label: subset hypothesis
span.quote: Some researchers adhere to what Kintsch et al. (1999) referred to as the “subset hypothesis,” which argues that a subset of the information that is actively maintained in working memory is that of which we are aware (cf. Cowan, 1999 ; O’reilly et al., 1999 ).

span.label: active contents or processes
span.quote: We adopt Baars & Franklin’s terminology (2003; see above), and refer to these as active contents or processes.

span.label: Pattern sets condition
span.quote: In the Pattern sets condition the locations of all the disks in a set follow a pre-determined pattern.

span.label: Broken Pattern and Control conditions
span.quote: In the yoked Broken Pattern condition the locations of the first four disks in a set follow the same pattern (e.g., zigzag), but the location of the fifth disk does not 2 , and in the yoked Control condition the locations of the first three disks are randomly determined, but the fourth and fifth follow the pattern.

span.label: implicit working memory
span.quote: Results from five studies show that WM can operate unintentionally and outside of conscious awareness, thus suggesting that the current view should be expanded to include implicit WM.

span.label: subset hypothesis
span.quote: the “subset hypothesis,” which argues that a subset of the information that is actively maintained in working memory is that of which we are aware

span.quote: The current study employs a 2 (Instructions: Implicit vs. Explicit; between participants) × 3 (Pattern: Pattern, Control, Broken Pattern; within participants), × 2 (Block) mixed design.

span.label: Block
span.quote: The main effect of block approached significance, F (1, 15) = 2.95, p = .10, suggesting that performance on the second block was a bit faster than on the first.

span.label: awareness
span.quote: Awareness was determined by whether participants could do so.

span.label: lag
span.quote: to assess the effects of repetition priming on words and non-words at lags of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 23, and 1050 intervening items

span.label: M = 528 ms vs. M = 565 ms — mean reaction time to the last disk in Pattern versus Broken Pattern sets in Study 1
span.quote: A 3 (Pattern: Pattern, Broken Pattern, Control) × 2 (Block) within subjects’ ANOVA revealed that, as hypothesized, RTs in the Pattern condition ( M = 528 ms, SD = 48) were considerably shorter than those for the Broken pattern condition ( M = 565 ms, SD = 62) with RTs for control sets falling in between ( M = 532 ms, SD = 48), F (2, 30) = 5.55, p < .01, MSE = 2.41, partial η 2 = .27.

span.label: 31 ms / 17 ms — size of the broken-pattern minus pattern RT difference for included (unaware) versus excluded (aware) participants
span.quote: First, whereas the difference between broken pattern and pattern RTs was 31 ms in the Included condition, it was only 17 ms in the Excluded

span.label: 20% — proportion of participants who correctly recognized the last pattern set, exactly the chance rate in a 5-alternative test
span.quote: Out of the remaining 30 participants only 5, or 20%, correctly recognized the set.

span.label: 24 (columns) by 18 (rows) — dimensions of the matrix into which the display screen was divided for disk locations
span.quote: In this paradigm the computer screen is divided into cells by a 24 (columns) by 18 (rows) matrix.

span.label: Twenty — number of participants in Study 1
span.quote: Twenty Hebrew University students participated in Study 1 in exchange for course credit or 15 Shekels (∼$3).

span.label: partial η 2 = .40 — effect size of the Pattern factor within the Implicit instruction condition in Study 4
span.quote: As hypothesized, the interaction consisted of a significant effect of Pattern in the Implicit condition, F (2, 32) = 10.75, p < .001, MSE = 1.12, partial η 2 = .40, and no effect of Pattern in the Explicit condition F = 1.1 (for means see Table 2 ).

span.label: M = 547 ms, SD = 84 vs. M = 561 ms, SD = 82 — mean RT to the fourth term in Pattern versus Broken Pattern number sets in Study 5
span.quote: As hypothesized, RTs for the fourth terms in the Pattern condition were significantly shorter than those in the Broken Pattern condition ( M = 547 ms, SD = 84 vs. M = 561 ms, SD = 82) t (25) = 2.35, p < .05.

span.label: 24 by 18 — the matrix of columns and rows dividing the screen
span.quote: the computer screen is divided into cells by a 24 (columns) by 18 (rows) matrix

span.label: five millimeters — disk diameter
span.quote: Small round disks (five millimeters in diameter) that are either empty (i.e., bagel-shaped), or full, appear in the different intersections of the matrix.

span.label: sets of five — stimuli per set, demarcated by a 1500 ms fixation point
span.quote: The stimuli appear in sets of five, which are demarcated from each other by a fixation point (a small square) that appears in the center of the display for 1500 ms.

span.label: 150 ms — interval between response and the next disk
span.quote: After each response the disk disappears and 150 ms later the next disk appears.

span.label: 10 patterns, 10 broken, 10 controls, 70 random — composition of each 100-set block
span.quote: In four out of the five studies we report, each block contains 10 different patterns, and their 10 yoked broken patterns and 10 yoked controls. The remaining 70 sets of each block are random.

span.label: 3.125 — average distance in matrix units between successive disks in experimental sets
span.quote: the average distance between disks in the experimental sets is 3.125

span.label: 528 vs 565 ms — Study 1 pattern against broken pattern reaction times
span.quote: RTs in the Pattern condition ( M = 528 ms, SD = 48) were considerably shorter than those for the Broken pattern condition ( M = 565 ms, SD = 62)

span.label: 20% — recognition accuracy in the five-alternative test, exactly chance
span.quote: Out of the remaining 30 participants only 5, or 20%, correctly recognized the set.

span.label: 31 ms vs 17 ms — the pattern effect in included (unaware) against excluded (aware) participants
span.quote: whereas the difference between broken pattern and pattern RTs was 31 ms in the Included condition, it was only 17 ms in the Excluded

span.label: partial η 2 = .20 and .14 — effect sizes for included against excluded participants
span.quote: the effect size in the Included condition was 50% bigger than that in the Excluded condition (partial η 2 = .20 and .14, respectively)

span.label: 20 excluded, 79 included — participants across studies 1–4 in the awareness comparison
span.quote: Twenty participants were excluded from analyses in these experiments (henceforth Excluded condition) and 79 were included (Included condition).

span.label: 15–30 s — duration of Maljkovic's implicit popout memory effect
span.quote: This effect lasts for 15–30 s, suggesting that the short term visual memory of the popout feature improves performance.

span.label: ∼140 ms at lag 0, asymptoting at approximately 50 ms at lag 4 — McKone's short-term repetition priming component
span.quote: starting from ∼140 ms at lag 0, and asymptoting at approximately 50 ms at lag 4

span.label: 200 ms / three SDs — the response-time exclusion window applied in every study
span.quote: Incorrect responses, as well as responses that were faster than 200 ms or slower than three SDs from the mean, were discarded from analyses (4.3%).

span.label: twenty — participants in Study 1
span.quote: Twenty Hebrew University students participated in Study 1 in exchange for course credit or 15 Shekels (∼$3).

span.label: fifty-four — participants in Study 4, the implicit/explicit contrast
span.quote: Fifty-four participants of the Hebrew University (36 females and 18 males) took part in this study, either for course credit or for 15 Shekels (∼$3).

span.label: twenty-eight — participants in Study 5, the algebraic replication
span.quote: Twenty-eight NYU undergraduates (mean age 19.4) participated in the study.

span.label: 25% of the trials — share of pattern and broken-pattern sets in Study 5
span.quote: These sequences accounted for 25% of the trials (12.5% each), and 75% of the sets were random.
